1.0.1.en: The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. [1]

1.0.2.en: About a century and a half earlier God had sent the prophet Jonah to warn Nineveh, the great city, of its destruction because of its corruption, and when the king and the people offered repentance, He forgave them and pardoned them. But soon they returned to their sins and fell into a worse state, until it was called "the bloody city" (Nah 3:1). And since they persisted in their evils in a hideous manner, He did not send them a prophet, but sent them a prophecy announcing the destruction that would come upon the city. As it is written in the book of Jeremiah: "At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; if it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them" (Jer 18:9-10).

1.0.3.en: This prophecy was fulfilled at the hands of Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus (Ahsuerus) or Xerxes.

1.0.4.en: * The meaning of the word "burden" is something of this kind: when God wishes to give the prophets insight, He often brings about a rapture of joy, causing a sudden change in their minds, so that in this state they receive knowledge of the future with deep fear. He calls it a "burden," and afterward the grace of the Spirit, where it seizes the mind of the prophet suddenly, turning him by a vision to the clear revelation of what is happening. He says the same thing here also: "The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite," as though he were saying: the mind of the prophet was suddenly seized by the grace of the Spirit and turned to contemplate those matters from which he learned what the fate of Nineveh would be, a matter that was presented to his hearers as teaching about what had been shown to him.

1.1.s.en: 2. Mighty in His mercies and in His wrath against sin:

1.1.0.en: 2 God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies. 3 The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet. 4 He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers: Bashan languisheth, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languisheth. 5 The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is lifted up at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein. 6 Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him. 7 The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him. 8 But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies.

1.1.1.en: God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth.

1.1.2.en: The LORD revengeth, and is furious.

1.1.3.en: The LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies. [2]

1.1.4.en: The prophecy came harsh and violent, yet full of tenderness and affection for the souls that cling to God. He begins by speaking of the Lord as a jealous God. This jealousy characterizes a husband toward his wife, so that he does not allow anyone to touch her or to wrong her, and it characterizes a king toward those who are subject to him in loyalty, so that he plans and works to protect them. So God's jealousy over man is a part of His love for him. He does not accept that anyone or anything should compete with Him to occupy the heart of man, His beloved.

1.1.5.en: His jealousy sometimes requires that He use the rod of discipline on man, because the latter wounds the relationship of mutual love by giving God his back and not his face.

1.1.6.en: He pours out this jealousy into the hearts of His faithful servants, so that they say with the Apostle Paul: "For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ" (2 Cor 11:2).

1.1.7.en: The heart of Phinehas the priest was kindled with jealousy for the holiness of the people and the tabernacle of the congregation when Israel committed harlotry with the daughters of Moab and worshipped their pagan gods, and one of them dared to bring a Midianitish woman to his brethren and enter with her into the tabernacle of the congregation. For when the priest thrust her through, the Lord said: "Phinehas... hath turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, while he was zealous for my sake among them, that I consumed not the children of Israel in my jealousy" (Num 25:11).

1.1.8.en: Elijah the prophet also says: "I have been very jealous for the LORD God of hosts: because the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword" (1 Kgs 19:10).

1.1.9.en: "God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth" [2]; He is jealous for His believers who walk in His way, who are sincere in their love for Him, and who trust in Him. If they sin, He disciplines them out of His jealousy and His great love for them; and He is an avenger not for His own sake but to protect His children, counting everyone who takes a stand of enmity against them as taking it against Himself personally. Therefore He says: "he reserveth wrath for his enemies" on behalf of His children.

1.1.10.en: God permitted the kingdom of Assyria to carry His people into captivity to discipline them, but Assyria thought that its idols were greater than God, and so it began to mock Him; and it went on humiliating the people of God.

1.1.11.en: * God is jealous, and He does not mock anyone with scorn. He does not mock like one who boasts of his own goodness, but He is longsuffering, yet He threatens.

1.1.12.en: Tertullian * My brethren, it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the Lord. And fearful is the face of the Lord against them that do evil (Ps 34:16)... Fearful is the ear of the Lord, which hears the voice of Abel speaking through his silent blood. Fearful are His feet, which step over the doing of evil. Fearful also is His filling of the universe, where it is impossible for any place to escape the work of God (Jer 23:24), even by flying up to heaven, or going down into hell, or fleeing to the uttermost east, or hiding ourselves in the depths, at the end of the seas (Ps 139:7-8). Nahum the Elkoshite stands before me trembling when he announces the burden of Nineveh, for God is jealous, and the Lord revengeth in His wrath against those who oppose Him.

1.1.13.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Observe, my beloved children, how the Lord our God is merciful and righteous, how compassionate and gentle with men, yet with great emphasis He "will not at all acquit the wicked" (see Nah 1:2). Although He welcomes the return of the sinner and grants him life, and leaves no room for any doubt, He does not act like one who judges harshly and utterly rejects the wicked, and refuses to give them counsel to bring them back to repentance. On the contrary, God says through Isaiah to the bishops: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, ye priests; speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem" (see Isa 40:1). Therefore it is fitting for you, when you hear these words of His, to encourage those who have sinned, to lead them to repentance, and to offer them hope. And it is not in vain that you reckon that you will share their transgressions at the expense of your love for them. Receive the penitent with joy, rejoice over them, and judge sinners with mercy and tender compassion. For if someone were walking on the bank of the river and stumbled, and you pushed him and threw him into the river instead of extending a helping hand to him, you would have committed the crime of murdering your brother.

1.1.14.en: Apostolic Canons The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked.

1.2.0.en: The LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet. [3]

1.2.1.en: God is slow to anger, waiting for man's repentance and return to Him. It was fitting for Assyria to realize that the victory it gained over the people of God was for the discipline of the people, so that it might take warning, abandon its idols, and believe in God, especially since they had previous experience in the days of the prophet Jonah. But instead of believing in God, Assyria used every means to treat God with contempt and blaspheme Him, and to humiliate His people in a savage manner. As the Apostle Paul says: "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God" (Rom 2:4-5).

1.2.2.en: God's longsuffering toward the wicked is not from any inability in power, for He is "great in power"; He delays, awaiting their repentance, and otherwise He will by no means acquit them.

1.2.3.en: "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever" (Ps 103:6-7).

1.2.4.en: The Lord showed Moses that He is merciful out of power and love, for the LORD descended in the cloud, and passed by before him, and proclaimed: "The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands..." (Ex 34:5-7). And Moses made haste, and bowed his head toward the earth, and worshipped.

1.2.5.en: God is longsuffering, but He will not at all acquit, that is, He does not leave evil alone to the end. Those who persist in their evil and do not repent, He will by no means acquit.

1.2.6.en: Just as man cannot withstand whirlwinds and storms and prevent the clouds, so he cannot stand before the wrath of God in arrogance and pride, but by repentance and humility he enjoys the divine mercies.

1.2.7.en: * "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy" (Ps 103:8). Why is He so longsuffering? Why is He plenteous in mercy? Men sin and live; sins continue and life continues. Men blaspheme every day, and He makes His sun to rise on the evil and on the good (Mt 5:45). In any case, He calls to amendment, He calls to repentance, He calls by His blessing of creation; He calls by giving time for life (opportunities for repentance), He calls through the reader (of the Word in the Church), and through the preacher, and He calls through the inner thought with the rod of correction, and He calls with the mercies of consolations. He is longsuffering and merciful. But take heed lest by abusing the greatness of God's mercies you treasure up for yourself wrath against the day of wrath, as the Apostle says (Rom 2:7).

1.2.8.en: St. Augustine * Again: "And I will establish my covenant with thee; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: that thou mayest remember, and be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more because of thy shame, when I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord GOD" (Ezek 16:62-63). Thus by these divine words He clearly indicates what was said in another place in the phrase: "And if He cleanses you, He does not make you righteous." For even the righteous, when they return from their former state after committing a sin, do not dare to open their mouths, but say with the Apostle: "I am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God" (1 Cor 15:9).

1.2.9.en: St. Jerome * "The Lord is longsuffering, and great in power, and will certainly not at all acquit" (Mic 1:3). He does not inflict punishment (discipline) immediately and suddenly, but after great longsuffering. You, O people of Nineveh, are witnesses to that, for when you practiced repentance you found salvation; after committing many evils for a long time you did not receive punishment for them. But when a people practice evils for a long time, He inflicts punishment on the impenitent. (The meaning of "will not at all acquit" is that He does not exempt from punishment those sinners who deserve it.)

1.2.10.en: Theodoret of Cyrus "The clouds are the dust of his feet." Here is a metaphor for the speed of chariots and surpassing horses, for they raise a cloud of dust, so that it is difficult to see them. So the Lord is like one who comes from heaven in His chariot, swift as lightning, and the clouds surround Him as the dust surrounds chariots and horses.

1.2.11.en: He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers.

1.3.0.en: Bashan languisheth, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languisheth. [4]

1.3.1.en: God created everything by a word, and by a word from Him He rebukes the sea and dries it, and dries up all the rivers that pour their waters into the seas. In ancient times He divided the Red Sea so that His people might cross as on dry land, and He made a way for them to cross the Jordan.

1.3.2.en: The seas and rivers, with all their powers, dry up at a word from Him, while man, in his extreme weakness, takes a stand of disobedience and rebellion against his Creator, who is longsuffering toward him and loves him!

1.3.3.en: If man thinks himself to be something, let him look at Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon, the regions marked by greenery and beautiful flowers, for they wither before the heat of summer or the frost of winter. Who then is man that he should stand before the Creator of time and the Ruler of the whole universe?

1.3.4.en: Bashan was famous for its green pastures (Joel 1:10), Carmel for its fields of wheat and vineyards, and Lebanon for its forests (Isa 33:9).

1.3.5.en: Tertullian sees here a prophecy about the Lord Christ, who rebuked the winds, so that they were stilled and the waves grew calm: [Here is a prophecy of Christ walking on the waters, which preceded His coming. The words of the Psalm were fulfilled by Christ's crossing the lake, for the Psalmist says: "The LORD is upon many waters" (Ps 29:3). When He scattered its waves, the words of Habakkuk were fulfilled, who said: "He numbers the waters as He goes" (Hab 3:10) LXX, and when He rebuked the sea and it was calm, the words of Nahum were also fulfilled: "He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry" (Nah 1:4), referring to the winds that had stirred up the sea].

1.4.0.en: The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is lifted up at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein. [5]

1.4.1.en: Who can stand before his indignation?

1.4.2.en: And who can abide in the fierceness of his anger?

1.5.0.en: His fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him. [6]

1.5.1.en: The divine wrath is likened to the fires of volcanoes and earthquakes that demolish rocks, melt hills, and destroy entire cities, and there is no possibility of standing before these natural phenomena. If rocks that seem firm, which no one can move, collapse before the fires of erupting volcanoes, how then will man stand before the fires of divine wrath?

1.5.2.en: "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, mine anger and my fury shall be poured out upon this place, upon man, and upon beast, and upon the trees of the field, and upon the fruit of the ground; and it shall burn, and shall not be quenched" (Jer 7:20).

1.5.4.en: A strong hold in the day of trouble.

1.6.0.en: And he knoweth them that trust in him. [7]

1.6.1.en: Lest anyone, even the Assyrians, think that God is a mighty avenger, the prophet stresses the goodness of God and His tenderness toward those who trust in Him.

1.6.2.en: When man is angry he loses his peace, his love, and his tenderness, but God in His wrath against evil is full of tenderness. The prophet Habakkuk says in his prayer: "in wrath remember mercy" (Hab 3:2). In His wrath against evil He waits to have mercy on the sinner if he reveals his true longing for repentance. While the wicked are terrified of meeting with God, those who trust in Him sing, saying: "The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him" [7]. The righteous see in the power of God a consuming fire that protects them, able to save them; He surrounds them and keeps them from every fiery dart aimed against them. St. Peter says: "The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished" (2 Pet 2:9).

1.6.3.en: * "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good" (Ps 106:1). You who commit grave sins and despair of salvation, and think that because of the gravity of your sins you cannot obtain pardon, I advise you, or rather the prophet advises you, to give thanks to the Lord, for He is good. Great are your sins, but great is the Lord who has compassion on you. Confess your sins to the Lord, repent, and do not despair of your salvation, for the Lord is merciful. Do not rely on your own strength but rely on the mercy of the Lord.

1.6.4.en: St. Jerome * "For the Lord is good," good not in the same way as the things He created are good. For God made all things very good (Gen 1:31), not only good, but also very good... If He made all these things good, what kind (of goodness) is that which made them...? How far can we speak of His goodness? Who can grasp what is in His heart, and understand how the Lord is good? Let us return to our souls, for we are not worthy to contemplate Him in Himself. And in hope that we may contemplate Him when our hearts are purified by faith, then we shall rejoice in the truth. Now, since we cannot see Him, let us look at His works so that we may not live without praising Him. Therefore I say: give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, sing to His name, for it is sweet... What is sweeter than the food of angels? How could God not be sweet, when man ate the food of angels? For men live on food that is not different. This is true, it is wisdom, it is the goodness of God, but you cannot enjoy it in the same way as the angels.

1.7.0.en: St. Augustine But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies. [8]

1.7.1.en: Some see in this phrase a prophecy of what would befall Nineveh from the army of the Medes and Babylon, where the army storms the city as though a flood had come upon it, and no one can stand before it. Others see that it is a prophecy of the conduct of this army when it took Nineveh by making a flood in the river that destroyed the wall of 20 furlongs (Furlongs, a measure of length equal to 220 yards or one eighth of a mile).

1.8.s.en: 3. The destruction of the kingdom of Assyria and its army:

1.8.0.en: 9 What do ye imagine against the LORD? he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time. 10 For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry. 11 There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the LORD, a wicked counsellor.

1.8.1.en: What do ye imagine against the LORD?

1.8.2.en: He will make an utter end.

1.8.3.en: Affliction shall not rise up the second time. [9]

1.8.4.en: Perhaps he is referring here to what Sennacherib and his deputy Rabshakeh did, who reproached the Lord of hosts and spoke of Him openly as a God unable to protect His people and unable to rescue them from the hand of the king of Assyria.

1.8.5.en: The prophet mocks the kingdom of Assyria, which thinks itself a great kingdom able to resist the great God in His power, and asks: What do you devise against the Lord? For your resistance is not against mortal men, but against the Almighty Lord.

1.8.6.en: "Affliction shall not rise up the second time"; for when Sennacherib king of Assyria tried to take Jerusalem, his army was destroyed and his two sons killed him on his return to his own country, so there is no room for him to repeat the attempt and try to take Jerusalem again. Some see that the meaning here is that once the army of Assyria is destroyed there is no room for destroying it again, for it does not rise again to fight anew!

1.8.7.en: * A father does not teach his son unless he loves him. And a master does not improve his disciple unless he sees in him signs of promise. When a physician comes and does not attend to the patient, this is a sign that he despairs of him. It is fitting for you to answer thus: since Lazarus received evil things in his life, I accept with joy the sufferings so that I may enjoy the glory to come for me. For affliction shall not rise up the second time (Nah 1:9).

1.8.8.en: St. Jerome * A bishop, priest, or deacon who falls into fornication, perjury, or theft is to be cut off from his priestly rank but not suspended, for Scripture says to you: [Do not take vengeance twice for the same crime with sorrow] (see Nah 1:9) LXX.

1.8.9.en: Church Canons * Here I think the ancient authorities followed the old law: "Thou shalt not take vengeance twice for the same thing" (Nah 1:9) LXX. For this reason also lay people (the people), when they are excluded from the place of the faithful, are restored from time to time to the rank from which they fell. But the deacon falls under a final penalty by being cut off from his rank, and the rank of the diaconate is not restored to him, but remains as a permanent punishment.

1.8.10.en: * Priests who commit a sin unto death are deprived of their rank, but they are not excluded from the communion of the laity (the people), for one is not punished twice for the same fault (Nah 1:9) LXX.

1.9.0.en: St. Basil the Great For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry. [10]

1.9.1.en: King Sennacherib and his men, as they reproach the Lord of hosts, are reckoned like dry thorns standing before a blazing fire, or like drunkards who do not know what they utter. They are like stubble fully dry, which the fire devours with extreme speed.

1.9.2.en: It is clear that these slain soldiers (185 thousand) shared with their leader his evil spirit and his mockery of the Lord God, and therefore the angel of the Lord struck them. This appears from the prophet's words: "folden together as thorns, and drunken." Each of them was strengthening the hands of the others in evil, and stirring them up to blaspheme God, so that they became like a mass of thorns that cannot be separated from one another, which the farmer burns together with fire. And they were like a company of drunkards, each urging the rest to drunkenness and mockery.

1.9.3.en: Thorns signify the wicked, for they are like thorns that seem harmful, but are dry and soon catch fire and become helpless ashes. "But the sons of Belial shall be all of them as thorns thrust away, because they cannot be taken with hands: but the man that shall touch them must be fenced with iron and the staff of a spear; and they shall be utterly burned with fire in the same place" (2 Sam 23:6-7).

1.9.4.en: Drunkards stagger and pretend to be brave, and boast of themselves as great, rich, and strong, though a man could make them fall with the tip of his finger.

1.9.5.en: Diodorus Siculus relates that when the enemy entered Nineveh, Sardanapalus burned his famous palace, and thus the prophecy of Nahum was fulfilled that they would burn like thorns.

1.10.0.en: There is one come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the LORD, a wicked counsellor. [11]

1.10.1.en: He directs the speech to Nineveh, from which Sennacherib came out uttering evil against the Lord, and so destroys himself as he destroys the city from which he came out.

1.10.2.en: He calls Rabshakeh the foolish counsellor who advised the men of war sitting on the wall not to trust in the Lord, for He is unable to rescue them out of the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria (Isa 36). He is a counsellor of destruction, because his reproach of the Lord of hosts led to the killing of one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army in one night by the angel of the Lord (Isa 37:36). Sennacherib himself was also killed by his two sons Adrammelech and Sharezer (Isa 37:38).

1.11.0.en: 12 Thus saith the LORD; Though they be quiet, and likewise many, yet thus shall they be cut down, when he shall pass through. Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more. 13 For now will I break his yoke from off thee, and will burst thy bonds in sunder. 14 And the LORD hath given a commandment concerning thee, that no more of thy name be sown: out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image: I will make thy grave; for thou art vile.

1.11.2.en: Though they be quiet, and likewise many, yet thus shall they be cut down, when he shall pass through.

1.11.4.en: I will afflict thee no more. [12]

1.11.5.en: The kingdom of Assyria was like a razor that mowed down kingdoms as hair is shaved from the head, and therefore the punishment came that it itself would be mowed down. It is written in Isaiah: "In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard" (Isa 7:20).

1.11.6.en: Since this army had previously defeated many cities that relied on their pagan gods, they stood before Jerusalem as men in safety and peace, proud of their multitude and strength, and behold, they are "cut down" like grass, and the destroying angel passes through them and humbles them at once, and they do not rise from this destruction to fall again into a new destruction!

1.11.7.en: By saying, "Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more," the Lord reveals His purpose in discipline, which is the repentance of the sinner in humility and abasement, so that the Lord may lift him up and set him on high in glory. Therefore it is said of the Lord: "For the Lord will not cast off for ever: but though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men" (Lam 3:31-33).

1.11.8.en: By saying, "Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more," God assures King Hezekiah that He permitted him and his people this siege so that the people might recognize their fault and offer sincere repentance in a spirit of humility. And the blow that would strike the army of Assyria besieging Jerusalem would be decisive, so that Sennacherib would not besiege it again.

1.12.0.en: For now will I break his yoke from off thee, and will burst thy bonds in sunder. [13]

1.12.1.en: The Lord assures King Hezekiah and his men that God will break the yoke of Sennacherib and his army and burst his bonds, for the army of the Assyrians was storming many of the cities and villages of Judah, doing as it pleased with them, while Jerusalem was unable to defend these places, being like a city bound and fettered. It will enjoy freedom, and the army of Assyria will not launch another attack, for its strength will fail with the killing of 185 thousand by the angel of the Lord, and the army will be as though extinct, with no power.

1.12.2.en: The yoke which Assyria laid is the tribute that Sennacherib imposed on Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:14).

1.12.3.en: And the LORD hath given a commandment concerning thee:

1.12.4.en: That no more of thy name be sown.

1.12.5.en: Out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image.

1.13.0.en: I will make thy grave; for thou art vile. [14]

1.13.1.en: The command has gone out to destroy his name, so that no one speaks of him any more as a conqueror and victor, and his reputation is scattered with the wind like dust that passes and does not return. By saying "out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image," he perhaps refers to the killing of King Sennacherib by his two sons in the house of Nisroch his god (Isa 37:38; 2 Kgs 19:37). This hideous crime showed Nisroch's inability to protect the one who worshipped him, and the people looked at this temple, defiled by the crime, and cut the images out of it and refrained from worshipping in it. Perhaps he refers here to the collapse of the kingdom of Assyria, where the enemy laid Nineveh waste and smashed the images of their gods, which they thought were the secret of their victory.

1.13.2.en: "I will make thy grave; for thou art vile": the house of Nisroch his god became a tomb for him, where he lay despised by his two sons who killed him treacherously, so that he was deprived even of filial love. Perhaps he means here the city of Nineveh, which became a grave for Assyria, since it was destroyed in a shameful manner.

1.13.3.en: When our God enters our hearts, we long that our name be sown no more, since we bear His name, and we sing, saying: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). He shatters the ego in us and establishes His divine Kingdom in us. Selfishness is buried as in a grave, and He takes away our vileness to grant us fellowship in His glories, and the heavenly ones sing: "The king's daughter is all glorious within" (Ps 45:13), and the Heavenly One Himself speaks to us: "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" (Song 4:7). "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?" (Song 6:10).

1.14.0.en: Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!

1.14.1.en: O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts.

1.14.2.en: Perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee.

1.14.4.en: As he announces to Jerusalem the loosing of her bonds, the breaking of the yoke of the army of Assyria, the destruction of its king Sennacherib, and the cutting off of the images of its gods, Nahum prophesies of what is greater, namely the salvation that the Messiah offers to the whole world. He sees in the Lord Christ the One who comes as upon the mountains to proclaim true, eternal, inward peace, reconciling mankind with the Father, turning our lives into unceasing feasts, and shattering and cutting off the enemy of good, so that he has no authority over the children of God, but he and his hosts and his devices and his works and his thoughts are cut off: "he is utterly cut off."

1.14.5.en: What are these mountains on which the feet of the herald of peace walk, if not the prophecies that prepared mankind to receive the Savior?

1.14.6.en: * Surely He brought good tidings to Zion and offered peace to Jerusalem. He goes up on a mountain, and there He spends the night in prayer (Lk 6:12). Therefore return to the prophets and learn from them His whole role. Isaiah says: "O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain" (Isa 40:9). "And they were astonished at his doctrine: for his word was with power" (Lk 4:32)... [I am present, when the hour comes, on the mountains, I bring the good news of peace, and I announce good] (see Isa 42:7). And as one of the Twelve (the minor prophets), Nahum, says: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace, hastening" (see Nah 1:15).

1.14.7.en: Tertullian * Let him who remembers the Gospel recall how He (the Lord) ascended from hell and breathed the Holy Spirit into the face of Judah, that is, the Jewish disciples, since they belong to the New Covenant, whose feast days have become spiritually renewed and cannot grow old. Moreover we have seen that the rest of the prophecy (Nah 1:14) has been fulfilled, for the Gospel destroyed "the graven image and the molten image," that is, the idols of vain gods, which are now consigned to oblivion in the grave.

1.14.8.en: St. Augustine * By speaking of the feet he means the coming of the Apostles who went about the world preaching the coming of the Kingdom of God. Their appearing enlightened mankind by showing the way to peace with God, for whom John came to prepare (Mk 1:3; Isa 40:3). This is the peace to which those who believe in Christ hasten.

1.14.9.en: Father Ambrosiaster * It is not only my words that make these things clear, but the prophet foretold it beforehand, crying out: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace" (Nah 1:15). And what is his message that he proclaimed, if not what he went on to declare to them, saying: "Keep, O Judah, thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows to the Lord. For they shall no more return to what is old. It is finished; it is utterly cut off. He has been lifted up who breathed in the face and delivered thee from affliction" (Nah 1:15; 1:2) LXX. And now: who is this who has been lifted up...? If you wish to know the truth and be rid of the claims of the Jews, look to our Savior who was lifted up and breathed into the face of His disciples, saying: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost" (Jn 20:22). For as soon as this (the crucifixion) was accomplished, the old things came to an end: the veil of the temple was rent (Mt 27:51), and the (Jewish) altar was shattered, and although the city had not yet been laid waste, the abomination of desolation (Mt 24:15) was preparing to sit in the midst of the temple, and Jerusalem and all those old ordinances were receiving their end.

1.14.10.en: * The day of the feast has drawn near to us again, in which, if we keep silent, we make it unholy, but it must be dedicated to prayer more than all days, and in it we keep the commandments. For although we are in distress from those who grieve us, and because of them we shall not tell you about this season (since it is not among His people), yet thanks be to God who comforts the sorrowful, so that we are not defeated by the evils of those who accuse us and keep silent; in our obedience to the voice of truth we cry out with you aloud on the day of the feast, for the God of all told them (Moses and Aaron) to speak to the people to keep the Passover, and the Spirit proclaims in the Psalms, saying: "Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day." And the prophet cries out, saying: "O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts" (Nah 1:15).

1.14.11.en: And I am not sending you the word as though you were ignorant, but I am declaring it to those who know it, that they may realize that although some divide us from one another, God gathers us together, for we keep the feast with the same feast, and we worship the same God continually.

1.14.12.en: And we do not keep the feast as spectators, knowing that the Apostle rebukes such people, saying: "Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years" (Gal 4:10), but rather we honor this great day because of the feast, so that we may please God, all of us who serve God in every place, by our common prayers. The blessed Paul announced such a joy as near, and in this he did not announce days but the Lord for whose sake we keep the feast, for he says, "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7), so that, contemplating the eternity of the Word, we draw near to Him to serve Him.

1.14.13.en: * My dear beloved, God has brought us again to the season of the Passover, and through His tender love He has gathered us together to keep the feast. For God, who brought Israel out of Egypt, even now still calls us to the Passover, saying through Moses: "Observe the month of Abib, and keep the passover unto the LORD thy God" (Deut 16:10), and says through the prophet: "O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows" (Nah 1:15).

1.14.14.en: For if God Himself loves the feast and calls us to it, it is not right, my brethren, to put it off or to keep it slackly, but we must come to it with zeal and joy, so that, beginning to rejoice here, our souls may long for the heavenly feast.

1.14.15.en: If we keep the feast here with vigor, we shall without doubt receive the perfect joy that is in heaven, as the Lord says: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer: For I say unto you, I will not any more eat thereof, until it be fulfilled in the kingdom of God" (Lk 22:15-16).

1.14.16.en: So we eat of it now, if it makes us understand the reason for the feast, and by our knowledge of the Savior we walk according to His grace, as Paul says: "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Cor 5:8). For in these days the Lord died, so that we may no longer long for the works of death! He gave His life, so that we may keep our lives from the snares of Satan!

1.14.17.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic * [Concerning monks] It befits us to observe the days mentioned in such a way that the rest may be beneficial and not harmful to the body and the soul. For the joy of any feast does not weaken the thorns of the flesh, and our savage enemy (Satan) cannot be quiet because of these days of rest. So that we may keep the traditions of the feast season, and not be subject to the rule of fasting... it is enough for us at this time to take food at the sixth hour (12 noon) instead of the ninth hour, without changing the quantity or kind of food, lest we lose the purity of body and goodness of soul that we obtained during the Great Lent...

1.14.18.en: We must be on guard with vigilance to the end, lest our souls grow faint because of temptations and we lose the purity of our chastity that we obtained, through rest and negligence at the time of the Paschal feast after continual striving throughout the Great Lent. Therefore we must not add anything to the kind or quantity of food, but even in the two names of the feasts we must abstain from these foods, lest our joy in the feast stir up in us an extremely deadly struggle because of bodily passions, and so we turn to sorrow. Then we would weep for the lost purity of our heart with the sorrow of endless remorse.

1.14.19.en: At the same time it befits us to strive lest we be rebuked with this warning: "O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows" (Nah 1:15). For if the days of the feast do not conflict with the continuance of our asceticism, we enjoy constant spiritual feasts.

1.14.21.en: Mighty are You in Your love!
